L12: It's January in Grand Rapids. Sam and Jen Miller insure their house with the twenty eleven H O three, and winter is about to test it.
Picture their house as a party: every cause gets in, unless it's on the banned list. For their couch and T V, only the sixteen named perils on the guest list get in. Not on that list? Not covered.
Or for critters: birds, rodents, insects, and animals an insured owns. The Millers' dog, Biscuit, chewed the back door? Not covered.
Quick check: seventy days vacant, then vandals. Covered?

Ordinance or law, earth movement like an earthquake or sinkhole, and water. Power failure off premises, neglect, meaning not protecting property at and after a loss, and war. Nuclear hazard, intentional loss, when an insured meant it, and governmental action, like seizure or destruction.
The adjuster comes. Insure to at least eighty percent of replacement cost, and house losses are paid at replacement cost, no depreciation.
Did over should is three quarters. The repair costs twenty thousand dollars, so he gets fifteen thousand dollars once it's fixed. That beats the A C V, twelve thousand dollars.
Tuesday's cave-in missed the old couch. But Sam could claim the snow crushed it. What should he do?
Busted. Now no insured gets Section one coverage, not even Jen.

Under eighty percent, it's the greater of A C V, or did over should times the loss. Fraud by any insured? Every insured loses Section one coverage, though in Michigan an innocent co-insured is covered for a fire loss, up to their own interest. Michigan requires payment within thirty days of proof.

The neighbors' house, insured under the twenty eleven H O three, has been vacant for seventy consecutive days. Then vandals spray-paint the walls. The vandalism loss to the house is: A: Not covered. B: Covered in full. C: Covered at fifty percent of the loss.
Accidental discharge from plumbing: the water damage is covered, plus necessary tear-out.
Until repairs are done, only A C V is paid, unless the loss is under five percent of the insurance and under two thousand five hundred dollars. twenty thousand dollars isn't.
Take the A C V now, then claim the rest: give notice within one hundred eighty days after the loss that you'll repair.
To claim the rest after taking A C V, Sam must give notice within one hundred eighty days after the loss.
Loss payment under the unendorsed twenty eleven form.
Concealment or Fraud: if any insured lies about or hides a material fact, no insured gets Section I coverage, honest Jen included.
L15: Rosa just bought a new car in Lansing. Her agent Dana has news: Michigan has rules.

Michigan's default liability limits: a quarter-million per person and a half-million per accident for injuries, plus a skinny ten grand for property damage. That's the least an auto policy issued after July first, twenty twenty may carry, unless the insured signs a form for lower injury limits.

Rosa's policy, issued in twenty twenty-six, starts at the defaults. Say she's sued for hurting three people in one crash. It pays at most two hundred fifty thousand dollars each, and five hundred thousand dollars in all.
Rosa reads the risks, signs, and gets fifty thousand dollars and one hundred thousand dollars.
Lower limits need the signed D I F S form. Blank form? Big defaults.
Saturdays, Rosa drives for a ride-share app. Michigan sets special minimums.
Logged on and available, no ride yet: at least fifty thousand dollars and one hundred thousand dollars bodily injury and twenty-five thousand dollars property damage, plus P I P and P P I.
Then a fender bender sends Rosa's car to the body shop.
Near Traverse City, a driver rear-ends Rosa's rental.
Ow! His insurer pays my P I P, right?
No. P I P is no-fault. Kitchen-table rule: first, the policies on your own table. Yours, your spouse's, or a relative's who lives with you.
So Rosa's own insurer pays. Key exceptions: hurt in your employer's vehicle? Its insurer pays. Motorcyclist hit by a car? The car owner's insurer first.

Another rental rule: on rentals of thirty days or less, if the renter's driving hurts someone, a rental company that wasn't negligent is liable as owner only up to twenty thousand dollars per person and forty thousand dollars per accident. Same numbers as the old limits, but still the law.
Who runs that plan? The Michigan Automobile Insurance Placement Facility, or M A I P F. Its main job? Meet Rosa's neighbor Walt.
Nobody would insure me the ordinary way.
Day ninety: Jay, Rosa's roommate who drives her car daily, has his license suspended, and it's final. Under Chapter thirty-two, how should the insurer cancel?
Too short! Twenty days, minimum.
What does Rosa say? One: Sure! I'm the policyholder, so we're covered. Two: No. I'll drive you to your date myself. Three: OK, but I'll ride along to keep you careful.

Rosa is giving a prearranged ride through a ride-share app. Michigan requires the liability coverage for that ride to be at least: A: fifty thousand dollars and one hundred thousand dollars bodily injury, plus twenty five thousand dollars property damage. B: two hundred fifty thousand dollars and five hundred thousand dollars bodily injury, plus ten thousand dollars property damage. C: five hundred thousand dollars combined single limit. D: one million dollars combined single limit.
Rosa's coworker, hurt driving the company's truck.

Under Chapter thirty two, how to cancel? One: Cancel, calling Rosa an unacceptable risk. Two: Cancel over Jay: first-class, twenty days ahead. Three: Cancel over Jay: certified, twenty days ahead. Four: Cancel over Jay: certified, five days ahead.
L14: Rosa gets the hospital bill for her arm. She insures her own car, but the crash was her fault. Who pays?
Her own policy pays first: Rosa's own P I P pays for her arm.
Rosa's P I P pays four kinds of benefits. Remember them: Michigan Winters Can Snow.

Work loss pays her lost income for up to three years after the accident, minus fifteen percent, because the benefit isn't taxed. So P I P pays eighty-five percent, unless you prove a smaller tax advantage.
Rosa's grandma renews her policy. She and Grandpa, the only other person at home, both have Medicare Parts A and B.
Memory trick: Medic-aid gets a little aid. Medic-are folks are allowed out, if the household is covered.
Rosa's slide wrecked a stranger's fence and dented a stranger's properly parked car. So her P P I pays for both.
Rosa's insurer says no: P P I won't pay for a moving car.
P I P pays for injuries without regard to fault, even when you caused the crash.
As a rule, your own policy pays first. Rosa insures her own car, so her own P I P pays her injuries, whoever caused the crash.
P I P pays for bodily injury without regard to fault. Rosa's own policy pays, even though she caused the crash.
P P I doesn't pay for your own car. That's for collision coverage. Rosa was over fifty percent at fault, so limited collision wouldn't pay; broad form would.
Rosa's hospital bills and lost wages.
A car Rosa rear-ends in Toledo, Ohio.
Someone to do Rosa's housework for a few months.
L13: First, Ed from next door trips on the Millers' sidewalk.
Ed sprained his wrist at the Millers' barbecue. So F pays his doctor bills. F: a friend's fall.
Watch out: never for you or regular residents of your household, except residence employees. Manual minimum: one thousand dollars per person.
F is for others, like guests: never you or your household, except residence employees.
Some catches: property of others won't pay if an insured thirteen or older did it on purpose, or for property an insured owns. Nor for damage from business or motor vehicles.
His twenty eleven H O three liability allows twenty five horses on the back: owned outboards totaling twenty five horsepower or less.
Owned sailboats twenty six feet or longer? Excluded too.
Done! Coverages E and F now apply to accidents with your boat.
Under the twenty eleven form, paid day care for unrelated kids is a business if it's an occupation, or paid over two thousand dollars in the twelve months before the policy period.
Quick check. Who is Business Pursuits made for?
Down the street, Dan and Ana own a house together. Dan sets it on fire on purpose. Ana had no part in it.
Both are insureds. That makes Ana an innocent co-insured: an insured who took no part in the act that caused the loss.
Their policy: a twenty eleven H O three with Special Provisions, Michigan. What should Ana claim?
Not quite. Ana gets only her own interest, never Dan's share.
Ana collects her share. Dan gets nothing, and the insurer may subrogate: go after him to recover what it paid.
Suing the insurer? Ana's twenty eleven policy allows two years after the loss, tolled, meaning paused, from notice of loss until formal denial. Michigan law requires at least one year.

F paid Ed's bills: it pays others' bills, not your household's, except residence employees. E defended Sam: damages plus defense, even for a groundless suit. On the twenty eleven form, property of others pays up to one thousand dollars. But not if an insured thirteen or older did it on purpose.

For liability, owned boats the H O three excludes, like Sam's, need the Watercraft endorsement. Slander needs Personal Injury. And in Michigan, Ana got her share: an innocent co-insured is covered for a fire loss, up to her interest.
Coverage F is medical payments to others. It never pays for you or regular residents of your household, residence employees aside.
Their son is a regular resident of the household. F doesn't pay for household residents, except residence employees.
Ed is a guest, hurt at the Millers' place with permission. F pays his medical bills incurred within three years of the accident.
Their fifteen-year-old trips and dents Ed's borrowed ladder.
An owned outboard over twenty five hp, owned before the policy period and never declared or reported, is excluded. No Coverage E.
Owned sailboats twenty six feet or longer are excluded too. That boat would also need the Watercraft endorsement.
Business Pursuits. Jen teaches for a school. This covers an insured's business activities when she isn't the owner or a partner, like teachers and salespersons.

Home Day Care Coverage. twenty eleven form: paid day care for unrelated kids is a business if an occupation or paid over two thousand dollars in the twelve months before the policy. Excluded; this adds limited coverage.

Business Pursuits is designed to cover the work liability of which person on the Millers' street? A: Priya, a salesperson employed by a furniture store. B: Mike, a partner in a downtown law firm. C: Kim, the sole owner of a hardware store.
Business Pursuits covers an insured's business activities when she isn't the owner or a partner, like salespersons and teachers.
What should Ana claim? One: Nothing. Dan's fire sinks us both. Two: The whole house, Dan's share too. Three: Prove domestic abuse first. Four: Her own share of the home.
L04: Sam and Jen Miller just bought a house in Grand Rapids. Now they're at Dana's desk.
Wait. Dana, whose side are you on: ours, or the insurance company's?
Consideration is what each side gives: the Millers, premium plus compliance with the policy's rules; the insurer, its promise to pay. Don't flip them.

Competent parties need legal age, in Michigan eighteen, and mental capacity. And the purpose must be legal: insuring a shipment of illegal drugs is unenforceable. A contract banned by statute is void or unenforceable.
Watch the two A's: adhesion is about who wrote it; aleatory is the unequal exchange that rides on chance.
The Millers ask to change a word in their policy. Dana says the insurer wrote it: take it or leave it. Which trait?
Some courts give the coverage an insured would reasonably expect: the reasonable expectations doctrine. Michigan declined to adopt it, but on the exam, that's still its name.
Sam relied on it, so the insurer may be estopped from canceling for late payment. The law says stop.

Its cousin, waiver, is a choice: you wave goodbye to a known right on purpose. Watch out: waiver is chosen; estoppel is imposed because someone relied. The twenty eleven homeowners form requires waivers in writing by the insurer.
Personal. The policy insures the Millers, not the house. If they sell, the policy can't be assigned to the buyer without the insurer's written consent.
Aleatory. An unequal exchange that depends on chance. One month of premium might buy a huge claim, or years of premium might buy nothing.

The Millers ask Dana to change a word in their policy. She says the insurer wrote it, so they take it or leave it. This shows the policy is: A: A contract of adhesion. B: An aleatory contract. C: A conditional contract. D: A personal contract.
Adhesion: the insurer drafts it, and the insured takes it or leaves it without bargaining over the wording. Aleatory is the unequal, chance-driven exchange.
L06: Dana sends Tony's application to the insurance company. An underwriter decides: accept the risk? How much insurance? At what rate?
Underwriters also watch the loss ratio across their book of business: incurred losses divided by earned premium. Your turn.
Physical: the property. Moral: dishonesty or a motive to profit from a loss. Morale: meh, careless because insurance will pay.
That's special, or open, perils, formerly called all risks. It covers all causes of loss except those the policy specifically excludes.
Coinsurance, coming later, can cut a claim payment on underinsured property. With blanket, it applies to the total value under that limit.

Depending on the policy and state law, A C V can also be fair market value, or the broad evidence rule, which weighs all relevant evidence of value. A functional replacement does the same job equally well, but it need not be identical.

Don't mix up these two. Agreed value sends coinsurance on vacation. Stated amount is a ceiling, not a promise: you get the least of three amounts. Under the twenty ten auto endorsement, those are actual cash value, the cost to repair or replace, and the stated amount.
Agreed value, a twenty twelve building and personal property form option for buildings like Tony's shop, suspends coinsurance until the agreed value expiration date.
The charred kitchen was a direct loss; the lost sales, consequential. A C V is often replacement cost minus depreciation. Stated amount is a ceiling; agreed value suspends coinsurance.
Indifference to loss because insurance will pay is morale hazard: an attitude, not dishonesty.
Carelessness because insurance will pay is morale hazard: an attitude problem, not dishonesty.
The insured's circumstances create a motive to profit from a loss: moral hazard.
Fire is a peril: the cause of loss. The oily rags by the furnace were the hazard: a condition that raises the chance of loss.
Code two: Joisted masonry. Masonry exterior walls, but a floor and roof that can burn, combustible. Tony's shop: masonry walls, wood floor and roof.
Extra expense results from the damage: an indirect loss.
Under the twenty ten endorsement, the insurer pays the least of A C V, repair or replacement cost, or the stated amount: here, twenty six thousand dollars before any deductible.
Least of three: A C V twenty six thousand dollars, replacement twenty eight thousand dollars, stated amount thirty thousand dollars. The endorsement pays the least.
L05: She sues Tony. In exam words, she's the plaintiff and Tony's the defendant.
Trial day. The jury finds Tony negligent and puts Rosa's economic damages at one hundred thousand dollars.
Three more kinds. Absolute is KABOOM: ultrahazardous, abnormally dangerous activities, like blasting or keeping wild animals. Being careful is no defense.
Next morning, Tony's employee Joey, shoveling Tony's walk on his shift, carelessly flings a chunk of ice through the barber's window.
Vicarious: liable for someone else's act. Nothing was ultrahazardous, and no product was defective.

What does Tony argue she gets? One: zero dollars: any fault means she gets nothing! Two: thirty thousand dollars: her thirty percent share. Three: seventy thousand dollars: not the full one hundred thousand dollars.
Blasting is ultrahazardous. Using every precaution is no defense: absolute liability.
L07: Roll the DICE: Declarations, Insuring agreement, Conditions, Exclusions. Definitions explain the words in quotes; endorsements change the game.
Who, where, when and how much: declarations. The promise: insuring agreement. The rules: conditions. The we-don't-cover list: exclusions.
Who's insured? Tony and his grandma co-own the pizzeria, and the policy names both: two named insureds.
Found it: duties after loss. One duty: give the insurer prompt notice. Tony calls right away.

Wednesday, the adjuster tallies seventy thousand dollars of fire damage to Tony's ovens and kitchen equipment. His twenty twelve property form insures them: limit sixty thousand dollars, deductible two hundred fifty dollars, no coinsurance penalty.
Equal shares: alike until a limit is used up. The trap: one hundred eighty-seven thousand five hundred dollars, the big policy's share by limits.
For Tony, that's injury away from his premises from his product, like takeout pizza that makes someone sick at home.

Fifty, one hundred, twenty-five: fifty thousand dollars per person, one hundred thousand dollars for all injuries, twenty-five thousand dollars for all property damage. Those are three separate caps per accident.

What a week! Roll the DICE: declarations, insuring agreement, conditions, exclusions. The first named insured pays the premium and gets notices and refunds. The deductible comes off the loss; the limit still caps the payment.
Declarations. Who, where, when and how much: the named insureds, the address and location, the policy period and the limits.
Insuring agreement. The insurer's promise to pay. It starts broad, and the exclusions and definitions narrow it.
Definitions. Words in quotation marks have special meanings, spelled out in the policy's Definitions section.
His policy's terms can be amended only by an endorsement the insurer issues. Tony may change them only with the insurer's consent.
Mexico is not part of the twenty eighteen P A P's policy territory.
L02: Two: cash back. Vic offers Rosa two hundred dollars back. Giving back premium or commission, or anything of value the policy doesn't specify, is rebating.
Three: a lie. Vic claims his insurer never loses money. Misstating a policy's terms or benefits, or an insurer's financial condition, is misrepresentation.
Is every gift a rebate? No. Michigan P and C has a gift limit: merchandise costing the insurer fifty dollars or less per calendar year is allowed. Cash back is not.

In Michigan, premiums Dana collects are fiduciary money: she holds them in trust for others. So are return premiums. They aren't hers, so they're segregated, or kept apart, and never commingled, or mixed, with her own.
Here's the trap: putting premiums in personal checking, even with a ledger, is commingling. And holding a refund for future premiums takes the insured's written OK.
The refund lands next to Dana's lunch money. Commingled!
Licensing law, in thousands: Oops one, didn't know. Knew five, knew or reasonably should have. Those are maximums per violation. Cap fifty per order.
Solo four, Squad ten: committing fraud risks four years; plotting it with a partner risks ten. Either way, up to fifty thousand dollars and you pay it back.
The office sign. Signs and general advertising don't count. Mail, hand delivery, or a website notice the online customer must acknowledge all work.

What a year! Twisting switches, rebating pays back, misrepresentation misstates. A P and C gift? Merchandise costing the insurer fifty dollars or less a calendar year. Premiums are fiduciary money: segregated, never commingled.
Fraud: up to four years solo, ten with a partner, and up to fifty thousand dollars either way. Privacy: think PAPER. Thirty days to opt out is reasonable, and notices are never solely oral.
Defamation. De-fame: a billboard on I ninety-four falsely shouting 'Rival Mutual is going broke!' to steal its customers. Spoken attacks count too.
Boycott. B C I: Bullies Can't Insure: Boycott, Coercion, Intimidation. Insurers agreeing to shun one agency's customers unreasonably restrain its business.
L01: Waive your fee if I buy through you?
A licensed agent's customary advice, or a Michigan attorney's, needs no counselor license.
Your turn. Contract signed May first, first application May tenth. When is Dana's appointment notice due?
A year later, the company, an auto and home insurer, wants to drop Dana: just eighteen home and auto applications in twelve months. She owns her renewal rights. Which move is legal?
Moving to Michigan with another state's license? Apply as a resident within ninety days, no prelicensing course or exam for lines held.

Legal name, address and email changes: thirty days. An assumed name: before you use it. For C E, twenty-four hours every two years, at least three of them ethics. And the ninety-day grace period: service and commissions only.
Her helper: solicitor. Solicits applications and collects premiums for Dana, a licensed resident producer. A sidekick with three L's: Leash, written contract, License, Letter, to the director.
What does Dana do? One: The contract's signed. Bind it now! Two: Wait until the company appoints her. Three: Bind it for fifteen days while she waits.

An insurer signs an agency contract with Dana on May first. Her first application to it goes in on May tenth. When must it file her notice of appointment? A: Within fifteen days of May first. B: Within fifteen days of May tenth. C: Within thirty days of May first. D: Within thirty days of May tenth.
Binding a new risk for that insurer needs its approval.
Rosa's auto policy with that company comes up for renewal. Dana renews it.
What does Dana do? One: Bind it. It's only a grace period! Two: Sign up for a C E class, then bind it. Three: Say no; keep servicing old customers. Four: Shut down: no service, no commissions.
Too cautious. In the grace period she may still service policies she already sold and receive commissions on them.
L00: It's like the height line at a ride: reach it and you're on. Her exam, P S I Series sixteen eighty-one, has one hundred fifty scored items and two point five hours. The cut score is seventy-four percent.
The four smallest, Businessowners, Workers' Comp, Other Coverages and Dwelling, still add up to twenty-seven items. Don't skip them.
In Michigan, the exam comes after prelicensing education, a required course: forty hours for combined property and casualty.
Nice try. A designation like C P C U would be.
Quick check: D I F S, Michigan's insurance department, just entered her application. How long does she have to pass?
Seat booked, Dana studies with this app. Every day, she taps Start today's session first.
She picks D, her best guess, jots thirty-seven on scratch paper and moves on.

The small four. Businessowners six percent, nine items, Workers' Comp five percent, eight items, Other Coverages four percent, six items, Dwelling two point five percent, four items. Together: seventeen point five percent, or twenty seven items.
Exam results are invalidated if prelicensing education wasn't completed before the exam.
Prelicensing education comes first. The certificate is valid for twelve months from completion: pass the exam within that window.
L03: Handle risk like a STARR: Share it, Transfer it, Avoid it, Reduce it, or Retain it. The five methods start with S, T, A, R and R: STARR, with two R's.

An ideally insurable risk is a CLEAN Deal, and Tony's fire risk is one. Calculable chance of loss: the insurer can estimate how often and how badly shops burn. Large numbers of exposure units: thousands of pizzerias. Economically feasible: an affordable premium. Accidental: an unintentional loss.
Quick check: the pool grows a hundredfold. What happens? Pick an answer.
Who protects Tony's insurer? A reinsurer: for a premium, it covers part or all of the insurer's liability. That's reinsurance: insurance for insurance companies.

Tony's insurer takes on thousands of shops, then passes part of that risk to a reinsurer. That makes the insurer the ceding company. Why buy? Capacity to write more, surplus relief, steadier results and catastrophe protection.
Quota share splits premium and losses at one percentage. Excess of loss pays only above the insurer's retention, up to a limit.
Quota share, a pro rata form, splits by one percentage. Excess of loss starts above the retention.

A reciprocal: unincorporated subscribers pooling risks, run by a manager called an attorney-in-fact. Lloyd's is a marketplace of underwriters, not an insurer. A M Best: A plus plus and A plus, Superior; A and A minus, Excellent.
A hazard is the condition; the peril is the cause of loss. Pure risk is generally insurable; speculative risk can bring a gain. Handle risk like a STARR. Ideally insurable risks are a CLEAN Deal.
Quota share shares premium and every loss at the same percentage. Help only above a retention is excess of loss.
Excess of loss pays the part of a loss above the ceding company's retention, up to a limit.
Mutual company. Owned by its policyholders. Every owner is an insured, and every insured is an owner. Memory hook: "My policy makes me an owner."
Reciprocal. An interinsurance exchange: picture neighbors swapping risks. It's an unincorporated group of subscribers who pool risks, run by a manager called an attorney-in-fact.
Who should Tony pick? One: The captive agent. Two: The direct writer's salesperson. Three: The independent agent.
L08: Coinsurance: insure at least a set share of the property's value, like eighty percent. Carry less, and every loss gets paid short, in proportion.
Watch out: people away, but belongings still there? That's unoccupied, like a furnished house while its owners spend four months in Florida. Look for the stuff.
The twenty twelve B P P has its own test: an owner's building is vacant unless at least thirty-one percent of its square footage is in use.
We're the named mortgagee. What do we do?
Apparent authority is what a reasonable person assumes from how the insurer presents her. A license alone gives neither.

Did over Should, times the Loss, minus the Deductible, capped by the limit. Under the twenty twelve B P P, vacant over sixty days: some perils out, the rest cut fifteen percent. Subrogation: after paying, the insurer recovers from the party liable.
A mortgagee can collect after a denial; a loss payee usually can't.

A building worth five hundred thousand dollars at the time of loss is insured for three hundred thousand dollars with eighty percent coinsurance and a one thousand dollars deductible. A one hundred thousand dollars covered loss occurs. What does the insurer pay? A: fifty nine thousand dollars. B: seventy four thousand dollars. C: seventy four thousand two hundred fifty dollars. D: ninety nine thousand dollars.
What should the bank do? One: Give up: his denial sinks us too. Two: Sue the owner and win in court first. Three: File a sworn statement within sixty days.
The mortgagee's claim stands if it reports known changes in risk, pays premium due on demand, and files a sworn statement within sixty days after notice.
L09: A floor, not a ceiling: policies may pay more. Coverage starts at twelve oh one A M standard time, where the property is.
In Michigan, one year after the loss, or the policy's longer period. And that clock can be tolled.

Tolled means paused: a deadline clock that stops running for a while, like a paused game clock. From the day the loss is reported until the insurer formally denies liability, your time to sue doesn't run.
The loss is payable within thirty days after proof of the amount of loss, unless the fire-loss withholding law applies. In some towns, part of a big fire payment is held back.

You live there, as owner or tenant. Own up to four units and live in one? Eligible, like Ana: she owns a three-unit building in Lansing and lives upstairs. A landlord living elsewhere? Not eligible, like Ben: he owns a rental house in Saginaw but lives elsewhere.
Next, each insurer's deductible: twenty percent of its prior-year direct earned premium. Above it, Uncle Sam pays eighty percent.
Under current law it ends December thirty-first, twenty twenty-seven, but extension bills were pending in twenty twenty-six: re-check.
Sunday's news: an insurer is insolvent. Its covered claims go to the Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association.
Quick recap. Fire policies: at least actual cash value, fire and lightning, twelve oh one A M. Minimum earned premium: pro rata or twenty-five dollars, whichever is greater.
In Michigan, pay within thirty days after proof. At least a year to sue, and that clock can be tolled. Appraisal: twenty days, then fifteen.
T R I A: each insurer's deductible is twenty percent of last year's premium, and the feds pay eighty percent above it. The guaranty cap spares P I P and workers' comp.
Coverage starts at twelve oh one A M standard time.
It takes effect at twelve oh one A M where the property is.
What should Sam do? One: Let the insurer's appraiser pick alone. Two: Ask the state insurance Director to pick. Three: Ask a circuit court judge in the county.
Rosa rents an apartment in Lansing and lives there.
The lifeboat. When a member insurer is insolvent, the Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association pays its covered claims.

Which claim is not subject to Michigan's five million dollars guaranty claim cap, statutory base? A: A homeowners dwelling claim. B: A commercial property claim. C: A general liability claim. D: A no-fault P I P claim.
L10: We're landlords! Now, how do we insure this place?

It insures a home for one to four families, whether or not it's the owner who lives there. Take the Millers' Lansing rental: they own it, but it's Rosa who lives in it. A two-family duplex could use one too.
Before you sign: what if a visitor slips on your icy steps and sues?
January: a visitor slips and sues. Even the Special Form has no liability coverage, so it pays nothing.
Coverage A fixes the house. The lost rent? Different letter.
In May, with Rosa back, a burglar pries open the back door and grabs the Millers' T V.
Here's the gap. In the D P two and D P three, damage by burglars is a named personal property peril. It covers the damage burglars do to covered property, but not theft.
Watch out: homeowners forms list theft. Dwelling forms add it by endorsement, picked by who lives there.
Pick by who lives there, not by price. Rosa does live there, but the named insureds, the Millers, don't.
The nineteen eighty eight D P one Basic Form: a short list. Extended Coverage perils and vandalism each need their own premium.
Only the D P three insures the dwelling and other structures on an open-perils basis.
The nineteen eighty eight D P one pays A C V. The D P two and D P three pay buildings at replacement cost if insured to at least eighty percent.

The Millers choose the two thousand two D P three. Which coverages does it insure on an open-perils basis? A: Dwelling, other structures and personal property. B: Dwelling and other structures only. C: Dwelling only.
L11: At a party, named perils is a guest list: not on it, no entry. Open perils is a banned list: everyone else gets in.
Watch out: open isn't everything. Exclusions, like flood, still apply.

Number peg: two Broad, a named list. Three Special, the house is open. Four, renters: the four walls aren't yours, so only Coverages C and D, no A or B. Five, high five: open on everything. Six, the condo unit. Eight, the eight track: older homes.

Rosa's grandma owns a condo in Traverse City. H O six is for condo owners and co-op shareholders. Its Coverage A covers her unit's alterations, appliances, fixtures and improvements, not the whole building.
The Millers get a twenty eleven H O three. Coverage A: the house, attached structures like their garage, and repair materials on site.
Attached is A, set apart is B, belongings are C.
Quick check: Sam's nine thousand dollars of gear burns in a storage fire. What's paid?
Right: one thousand five hundred dollars for the jewelry, two hundred dollars for the cash.
Sam spills a can of paint on the hardwood floor. It isn't a named peril, so this form won't pay for the floor.
Set apart from the house by clear space: an other structure, Coverage B.
Materials and supplies on or next to the premises, for repairing the dwelling, are Coverage A.
A garage set apart by clear space is an other structure: Coverage B.
What should Sam claim? One: A new maple, under the trees coverage. Two: Skip it: wind-blown trees get nothing. Three: Claim tree removal: the car is blocked in.
L16: The six parts? Rosa's question to Gramps: Let Me Use Dad's Dodge, Gramps?

Each word stands for a part, in order. Part A is liability, B is medical payments, and C is uninsured motorists. D is damage to your auto, E is duties after an accident or loss, and F is general provisions.
Near Lansing, a deer leaps in front of Rosa's car, and she hits it. Bambi is not a collision: hitting a deer, or a bird, is other than collision.
Rolled over, or hit a vehicle or object? Collision. An animal, weather, a falling object, fire or theft? Other than collision.
Broad form pays regardless of fault, and waives the deductible if the driver wasn't substantially at fault. Over fifty percent at fault? It pays, minus the deductible.
Smart move. In October, a thief steals Rosa's car.
Time logged into a ride-share app as a driver is excluded, rider or not. Not excluded: share-the-expense car pools and volunteer driving.
One night, an unknown driver rear-ends Rosa's car and speeds off. She's seriously hurt, so she makes an uninsured motorists claim.

Garagekeepers covers customers' autos left in a shop's care while it services, repairs, parks or stores them. For example, Tony's van is at Gus's repair shop for brakes. If it's damaged there, Gus's garagekeepers may pay, depending on its basis.
Gus carries garagekeepers Comprehensive. Which basis fits?

Hail hits. Tony's own insurer pays first, and Gus's policy pays only what's left.
Finally, big rigs, like the semi hauling Tony's flour. The Motor Carrier Act of nineteen eighty sets federal minimum limits.

Michigan P I P and P P I. The Business Auto form has no P I P section. In Michigan, P I P and P P I endorsements add those no-fault benefits. Symbol five marks owned autos subject to no-fault.

L18: A package is common declarations and conditions, plus coverage parts. One part alone is monoline; two or more make a package.
Now Tony's C G L, short for commercial general liability, twenty thirteen edition. Monday, a customer trips on a torn mat, breaks her ankle and sues.

Under the twenty thirteen claims-made C G L, the basic tail is free and automatic. It gives sixty days for occurrences never reported, and five years for those reported no later than sixty days after the end.
Neither tail covers injury after the policy ends.
A tail is like leaving the porch light on after a party that started at the retro date. Late knocks still get answered, but only from guests who were at the party, never from new arrivals.
Grace reports it tonight. When the guest sues in August, the basic tail covers it: reported in time, so five years.

A package is common declarations and conditions plus two or more parts. A is injury and damage, B the four P's, C med pay: no fault needed, but a one-year clock. Supplementary payments ride on top: up to two hundred fifty dollars for bail bonds, two hundred fifty dollars a day for lost earnings.
Coverage part: general liability. Tony's liability coverage. Coverage A, for one, pays injury and damage he legally owes others, plus defense. Two parts in one policy: a package.
Coverage C pays only expenses incurred and reported within one year of the accident. Fourteen months is too late.
Property damage that Tony legally owes for is Coverage A.
The rival's slogan suit against Tony.
Contractor's finished railing at a client's hurts a guest.
Reported before the policy ends, or no later than sixty days after, an occurrence gets the free basic tail: claims can come up to five years after.

Spoilage covers perishable stock for the causes you choose: Breakdown or Contamination, or Power Outage. Which one, Tony?
The association's form is primary and waives subrogation; a unit-owner's is excess. Builders risk covers buildings going up; legal liability, others' property in your care.

What a year! Broad adds a Michigan winter: falling objects, the weight of snow and ice, and water damage. Only Special covers theft. Vacant over sixty days? Some losses out, the rest cut fifteen percent. Coinsurance: Did over Should, times the loss, minus the deductible.
After a fire, a Traverse City dentist equips a temp office.
The form's coinsurance condition doesn't apply to it.
Coinsurance can apply to Business Income, not Extra Expense.

His own tools: contractors equipment. What he's installing: an installation floater.

Coverage F insures Grandma's own farm personal property. The trampled corn belongs to the neighbor.

Hired autos, and autos you don't own, like an employee's car, used in your business: Hired and Non-Owned Auto Liability.
